https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq56.text: Figure caption, Watch: Record rainfall causes flooding in Japanâs Chiba region By Kelly Ng Â and Â Kurumi Mori ,Â Tokyo correspondent Published 14 August 2026, 05:54 BST Updated 13 minutes ago At least six people have died and five others are wounded in eastern Japan as record rainfall pummelled the Chiba prefecture near the capital Tokyo. The rains, which authorities have described as "unprecedented", cut power to more than 20,000 households while 7,000 travellers were stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport. Local authorities issued a level five emergency warning, its highest alert, on Thursday. This was downgraded to a level four by Friday morning, but they continue to warn of landslide and flooding risks. The deluge comes after a series of storms swept through Japan and neighbouring countries this week, in what's been forecast to be an unusually active typhoon season. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Cars were left abandoned in the streets of Oamishirasato, in Chiba Japan's Meteorological Agency said the most recent deluge was brought by warm, humid air flowing into the country's east that combined with cold air above to make atmospheric conditions extremely unstable. The rains are expected to last through late on Friday. "This case was an extremely unusual situation, even by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday morning. "I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this." Chiba, which sits right next to the capital city of Tokyo, has logged more than 100mm of rain per hour since Thursday afternoon, authorities say. This is about three times the average rainfall in August, and the highest volume of precipitation ever recorded in the country. Authorities would prioritise saving lives and persist with rescue efforts, Kumagai added. At lest six people have died, according to reports from public broadcaster NHK, Kyodo news agency and Asahi newspaper. Among those killed was a woman who died inside her car submerged on a flooded road, authorities said. Two others collapsed along the streets and later died. The Japan Meteorological Agency earlier described the situation as an "unprecedented level of heavy rain". Several rail services remain suspended on Friday morning while some major highways are also shut. More than 100,000 households have been asked to evacuate on Thursday after the rain triggered landslides and power outages. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Thousands were stranded overnight at Narita as the storm disrupted transportation to and from the airport All flights are scheduled to operate normally on Friday, a spokesperson from Narita airport said. Flag carrier Japan Airlines said some of its flights may be delayed but that it does not expect any cancellations. Passengers were stranded at metro stations, while around 1,800 people spent the night at the Chiba Prefectural Government building. A woman in Chiba's Ichikawa city told NHK the rain "happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise". "The power is out so I'm worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days," she said. Meanwhile in the Philippines, authorities have again shut schools and government offices are again shut in most of the country's north, citing the threat of floods. Earlier this week, Japan, the Philippines and China were hit by back-to-back storms â Dolphin, Chan-Hom and Peilou â churning across the region at the same time. Dolphin brought heavy rain to Japan's Okinawa island, cutting power to tens of thousands of buildings, toppling trees and cancelling flights. Over the weekend, Chinese authorities evacuated more than a million people from their homes as Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, made landfall in the country's east. https://www.politico.eu/article/meet-the.text: STOCKHOLM — Sweden’s nail-biting election battle will come down to which prime minister candidate can cobble together a coalition with majority support in a new parliament that looks likely to be split almost equally between left and right. And that makes Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist perhaps the most powerful woman in the country, for now at least. She is the leader of the small, liberal Center Party, which is projected to win 25 seats in Sweden’s 349-member parliament. Advertisement Advertisement Those two dozen or so votes in the Riksdag would be invaluable to both rivals for the job of prime minister. Center-right incumbent Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is scrambling to try to keep his job and won’t concede until he has tried everything. He’s now widely expected to try to tempt Thand Ringqvist to join his bloc, perhaps offering sweeteners in keeping with her business-friendly agenda, and arguing that she doesn’t really want to work with socialists and the far left. Until now, she has been aligned with the opposition side — a bloc of four parties led by center-left Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson. The most likely first step remains for the Center Party to work toward a deal with Andersson’s left-wing grouping. But, like everything else in Sweden’s coalition-building process, it’s complicated — and there’s history. Thand Ringqvist tends to make one overriding point above others when asked which parties she could team up with: She won’t let politicians on the extreme edges of the left or the far right force the mainstream parties to dance to their tune. “We are ready to form a government with others,” she said as votes were being counted on election night. But she warned: “The fringes should not dominate a government.” Advertisement Advertisement In practical terms, she has refused to work with the far-right, anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, who Kristersson needs on his side to have any hope of winning. But she has also ruled out working with the former communists in the Left Party, who Andersson is likewise dependent upon for a majority. The Left Party, which will be emboldened by a bigger haul of seats, has said the price of its support is having ministers in the government — and that’s too far for Thand Ringqvist. Unlike Kristersson, who has led his Moderate Party since 2017, or Andersson, who was prime minister and lost power in 2022, Thand Ringqvist is not a veteran operator with a long record of deal-making in parliament. The 54-year-old former lobbyist was first elected in 2022 and has been leader of her party only since November last year. For now, she is keeping her counsel. Votes are still being counted, and the final seat tally won’t be known before Wednesday. Parliament won’t meet to vote on who could be prime minister until Sept. 29 at the earliest. In time, however, she will have to choose. There are many crisscrossing red lines in play among the eight parties — and leaders, in the end, tend to find ways to compromise. If they can’t, Sweden may not get a government at all. Advertisement Advertisement
